questionStem: A 62-year-old woman comes to the physician because of two episodes of vaginal bleeding during the past 3 weeks. Menopause occurred 12 years ago. She has hypertension treated with an ACE inhibitor and type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with oral hypoglycemic agents. She has no history of abnormal annual Pap smears. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 66 kg (145 lb); BMI is 25 kg/m². Pelvic examination shows a normal cervix and uterus with blood at the cervical os. A 6 × 8-cm left ovarian mass is palpated. Pelvic ultrasonography confirms the results of physical examination. An endometrial biopsy specimen shows atypical complex hyperplasia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Vaginal bleeding in a postmenopausal woman should raise suspicion for malignancy, including uterine or ovarian carcinoma. Ovarian sex-cord stromal tumors are a group of neoplasms which may secrete sex hormones, including estrogen or testosterone. Granulosa cell tumors are the most common sex-cord stromal tumor and present with an adnexal mass and evidence of estrogen excess such as breast tenderness and uterine bleeding. Estrogen excess is a known risk factor for atypical endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial carcinoma. In the case of granulosa cell tumor, ultrasonography may reveal a large, complex ovarian mass which may contain septations or cysts. Histologic diagnosis is made by biopsy; identification of Call-Exner bodies is considered pathognomonic. Granulosa cell tumor is treated with surgical resection and may require adjuvant chemotherapy in advanced cases.
incorrectExplanation: Brenner tumors (Choice A) are rare tumors derived from ovarian transitional epithelial cells. Presenting findings include an adnexal mass with a tan to yellow, firm gross appearance and cells containing nuclei with grooves on light microscopy. Brenner tumors are not hormone-secreting and are less likely to present with atypical vaginal bleeding in a postmenopausal woman. Ovarian carcinoma (Choice C) and ovarian fibroma (Choice D) both may present with a palpable adnexal mass. However, neither of these entities secrete estrogen and are unlikely to lead to atypical endometrial hyperplasia. Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor (Choice E) is a sex-cord stromal tumor derived from testosterone-secreting Sertoli-Leydig cells. Patients typically present at younger ages and may develop signs of androgen excess and masculinization.

questionStem: A 28-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, has been amenorrheic and has had hot flashes for the past 6 months. She takes thyroid medication for chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis (Hashimoto disease). After using an oral contraceptive for 2 years, she discontinued taking it 3 years ago. Serum studies show: Follicle-stimulating hormone 62 mIU/mL Estradiol 15 pg/mL (N=20–60) Thyroid-stimulating hormone 1.5 μU/mL Prolactin 5 ng/mL Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
correctExplanation: Autoimmune ovarian failure, also known as primary ovarian insufficiency, classically presents in a woman of reproductive age with anovulation, amenorrhea, and infertility. It can also present with signs of early menopause, such as hot flashes, night sweats, and irregular bleeding. It is caused by autoimmune inflammation and destruction within the ovaries, leading to a decrease in estrogen production, diminished follicle reserve, and loss of ovarian stromal cells. Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) are appropriately increased because of the lack of negative feedback from estrogen on the anterior pituitary, as is seen in this case. It is most often idiopathic but is more common in women with karyotype abnormalities or other autoimmune diseases such as chronic lymphocytic (Hashimoto) thyroiditis.
incorrectExplanation: Hypothalamic dysfunction (Choice B) can also lead to anovulation and amenorrhea by virtue of decreased gonadotropin-releasing hormone, which subsequently leads to decreased FSH and LH concentrations. It is a common cause of amenorrhea or anovulation in young athletes. Inadequate control of hypothyroidism (Choice C) can also cause amenorrhea and infertility. However, the patient’s TSH concentration is within normal limits. This indicates that her thyroid supplementation is adequate. Post-pill amenorrhea (Choice D) is a common period of anovulation and amenorrhea following discontinuation of long-term oral contraceptive medications. Combined oral contraceptives contain estrogen and progesterone, and their steady effects on the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis prevent ovulation or implantation of a fertilized oocyte, thereby preventing pregnancy. After discontinuing oral contraceptives, it may take several months for the normal hormone cycle to resume. However, this patient discontinued oral contraceptives three years ago, making persistent post-pill amenorrhea unlikely. Pure gonadal dysgenesis (Choice E) is defined by the absence of functional ovaries (eg, atrophic gonads). It presents with amenorrhea and absence of secondary sexual characteristics, and results of laboratory studies will show decreased estrogen concentration and increased FSH and LH concentrations. As this patient previously was able to conceive, she does not have pure gonadal dysgenesis.

questionStem: A 35-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, with chronic hypertension has spontaneous onset of labor at 39 weeks' gestation. After 4 hours of regular contractions and a second stage of 5 minutes, she spontaneously delivers a 3650-g (8-lb 1-oz) newborn under epidural anesthesia. Approximately 2 minutes after separation of the placenta, she develops apnea, cyanosis, and severe hypotension. During the unsuccessful resuscitation, the patient develops bleeding from the vagina and venipuncture sites. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare and potentially fatal complication of childbirth caused by amniotic fluid entering the maternal circulation. It most commonly occurs during delivery or in the immediate postpartum period. It presents with acute onset apnea, cyanosis, and circulatory collapse leading to altered mental status or unconsciousness. It is further associated with diffuse bleeding from venipuncture sites, the vagina, or a cesarean delivery incision due to disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (DIC). Signs of fetal distress can also occur if the fetus remains in utero at the time of occurrence. Vital signs will disclose tachycardia, hypoxia, and severe hypotension. The patient can quickly decompensate into cardiovascular collapse and cardiopulmonary arrest. Treatment is generally supportive, with patients often requiring fluids or blood products and mechanical ventilation. The maternal and infant mortality rate is high.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E.

Aspiration (Choice B), the inhalation of oropharyngeal or gastric contents into the airway, most commonly occurs due to dysfunction in the swallowing mechanism. Aspiration would be unexpected and unlikely in this patient without emesis, neurologic dysfunction, or oropharyngeal neuromuscular or structural impairment, especially without such an event reported in the history.

Cerebral infarction (Choice C) classically presents with unilateral neurologic deficits depending on the vascular territory involved. Risk factors include hypertension and pregnancy, as well as hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking, and family history. While the patient does have risk factors for cerebral infarction, it does not describe her clinical condition.

Myocardial infarction (Choice D) classically presents as substernal or left-sided chest pain radiating to the arm or jaw, shortness of breath, diaphoresis, and nausea, but it can also present nonspecifically. It can be complicated by cardiogenic shock, leading to severe hypotension and possibly cyanosis. However, it would be unlikely in this young patient with hypertension as her only risk factor, particularly in the absence of chest pain or other symptoms.

Septic shock (Choice E) is a term used to refer to decreased organ perfusion that occurs from an overwhelming infection. Septic shock is a form of distributive shock, and is classically diagnosed with fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, and signs of infection on examination, as well as leukocytosis and lactic acidosis. The presentation is less abrupt (hours to days) in comparison to amniotic fluid embolism.

questionStem: A 52-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of urinary urgency. She often has a strong urge to void but passes only a small amount of urine. Sometimes, she is unable to reach a bathroom quickly enough after feeling the sudden need to void. She says she often feels hot at night and occasionally during the day. She has not had any other symptoms. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Her last menstrual period was 12 months ago. She is not sexually active. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 68 kg (150 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m². Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.7°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows moderate tenderness and vaginal atrophy. The uterus is normal sized. There are no vulvar, vaginal, or cervical lesions or adnexal masses. The remainder of the examination, including rectal examination, shows no abnormalities. Test of the stool for occult blood is negative. A wet mount preparation of vaginal fluid shows numerous leukocytes. Urine culture is negative. Her postvoid residual volume is 50 mL. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings?
correctExplanation: Estrogen deficiency in menopause can cause atrophy and inflammation of the vagina and urethra, leading to an overactive bladder (urgency, frequency, and urge incontinence). This inflammation can result in leukocytes within the urine and vaginal fluid in the absence of infection. Symptoms of hot flashes and last experiencing a menstrual period over 1 year ago, as experienced by this patient, are consistent with menopause and associated estrogen deficiency. Pelvic examination typically discloses vaginal atrophy and tenderness without other abnormalities. In addition to any condition causing urinary tract irritation or inflammation, urge incontinence can also be caused by detrusor muscle spasticity or instability from neurologic injuries (eg, neuropathy, stroke, trauma, multiple sclerosis). Treatment options for urge incontinence include bladder training (eg, timed voiding and relaxation techniques), Kegel exercises, and antimuscarinic medication (eg, oxybutynin). In general, supplemental estrogens are no longer widely recommended due to the increased risk of gynecologic and breast malignancies and venous thromboembolic disease.
incorrectExplanation: Patients with atonic bladder (Choice A) possess underactive or flaccid detrusor muscles, which results in incomplete emptying and urinary retention as evidenced by an increased post-void residual bladder volume (not seen in this patient). Consequently, patients can experience overflow incontinence as intravesical hydrostatic pressure eventually overcomes internal and external urinary sphincter closing pressures. Atonic bladder can result from neurologic injuries. Bladder outlet obstruction (eg, benign prostatic hyperplasia) is another cause of overflow incontinence, though is only seen in men. Prolapse of the pelvic floor (Choice C) results in stress incontinence, or incontinence that is triggered by an increase in intra-abdominal pressure (eg, lifting, sneezing, Valsalva maneuver). Stress incontinence results from urethral hypermobility caused by pelvic floor prolapse or intrinsic sphincter deficiency. Risk factors for women include multiple vaginal deliveries and obesity. Trichomoniasis (Choice D) is a sexually transmitted infection that causes vaginitis and cervicitis in women and urethritis in men. Similar to estrogen deficiency, trichomoniasis can lead to overactive bladder. Trichomoniasis presents with green, malodorous vaginal discharge and motile trichomonads on wet mount, neither of which are seen in this patient. Urinary tract infection (Choice E) can present with overactive bladder. Patients generally also experience dysuria and suprapubic pain. This patient's urine culture was negative, essentially ruling out an infection.

questionStem: A sexually active 21-year-old college student requests an oral contraceptive. There are no contraindications based on her medical history. In addition to a Pap smear, which of the following screening tests is most appropriate?

choices.C: Measurement of fasting serum glucose concentration

correctExplanation: Testing for Chlamydia trachomatis, as well as for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, is recommended by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) for all sexually active patients under 25 years old. C. Trachomatis is a sexually transmitted infection that classically presents with urethritis, dysuria, and urethral or vaginal discharge. However, it can also be asymptomatic. Complications include cervicitis, epididymitis, reactive arthritis, and pelvic inflammatory disease. Gram stain of the urine or urethral/vaginal discharge typically does not reveal organisms, as C. trachomatis is an obligate intracellular organism. Diagnosis is made with a nucleic acid amplification test, and treatment consists of either azithromycin or doxycycline in combination with ceftriaxone, with the latter covering a potential N. gonorrhoeae coinfection.
incorrectExplanation:
Liver function tests (Choice B) would not be indicated in this patient. The patient has no risk factors for or symptoms related to liver dysfunction. A baseline level is not necessary prior to initiating oral contraceptives, as liver toxicity is an exceedingly rare adverse effect of oral contraceptive therapy.

Measurement of fasting serum glucose concentration (Choice C) is used to diagnose diabetes mellitus. Common symptoms include increased thirst, frequent urination, weight loss, fatigue, and frequent infections. The patient does not have signs or symptoms of diabetes and measuring serum glucose concentration is not warranted based on USPSTF guidelines for her demographic.

Assay for serum HIV antibodies (Choice D) to screen for HIV infection may eventually be appropriate, as the USPSTF and the Center for Disease Control recommend that everyone between the teenage years and age 65 be tested at least once. Those at higher risk (men who have sex with men, or those with multiple sexual partners, having sex in exchange for money or drugs, or using condoms inconsistently) should be screened more frequently. This patient would benefit more from testing for C. trachomatis at this time, as it is a more common infection and more frequently presents asymptomatically, though HIV testing should also eventually be performed.

The serologic test for syphilis (Choice E) is not recommended in asymptomatic patients. Syphilis has a multitude of presentations depending on its stage. Primary syphilis can present with a genital lesion that is nonpainful, while secondary syphilis presents with a maculopapular rash and condyloma lata. Tertiary syphilis, the most advanced form, has symptoms of neurosyphilis (eg, tabes dorsalis, Argyll Robertson pupil, ataxia) and aortitis. The patient is not experiencing any of these symptoms.

questionStem: A 32-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, at 30 weeks' gestation is brought to the emergency department because of pain in the right mid abdomen for 12 hours; she has had one episode of diarrhea since that time. Her temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F). Physical examination shows diffuse tenderness in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen with minimal guarding. Rectal and pelvic examinations show right-sided tenderness. Her leukocyte count is 14,000/mm³ with a shift to the left. Ultrasonography of the abdomen shows fluid in the right paracolic gutter; the appendix cannot be visualized. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Appendicitis typically presents with right lower quadrant abdominal pain that is often periumbilical at onset, with associated nausea, anorexia, fever, leukocytosis, and tenderness to palpation in the right lower quadrant on examination. In pregnancy, due to the location of the enlarging uterus, the appendix may be displaced superiorly as compared to that of a nongravid patient. This displacement limits the classic history and physical examination, which rely on a right lower quadrant position of the appendix. For example, initial periumbilical pain is attributed to vague, visceral innervation of the appendix being referred to the midline; once inflammation affects the parietal peritoneum, the pain becomes well-localized to the right lower quadrant, hence, the migratory character. McBurney point, a sensitive location for tenderness on palpation, is located at one-third the distance between the inguinal ligament and the umbilicus because this is the common position of the appendix. When displaced cephalad, the parietal peritoneal inflammation may no longer occur at the McBurney point, even migrating as far as the right upper quadrant, mimicking diagnoses such as cholecystitis. Diagnosis is facilitated by CT scan (though less ideal in pregnancy due to the risk of teratogenicity to the fetus), MRI, or ultrasonography, which may show appendiceal enlargement, the presence of an appendicolith, appendiceal wall thickening, or periappendiceal fluid. Fluid in the paracolic gutter is suggestive of appendiceal rupture or perforation and is typically accompanied by rising fever and leukocytosis. Immediate surgical exploration and appendectomy is indicated to prevent significant maternal and fetal complications including peritonitis, sepsis, and death.
incorrectExplanation: Cultures of the stool (Choice A) are appropriate for the diagnosis of infectious enterocolitis, which may present with abdominal pain, fever, and leukocytosis. However, infectious enterocolitis would generally not present with focal right lower quadrant abdominal pain, or fluid in the paracolic gutter. Barium enema (Choice B) and sigmoidoscopy (Choice D) may be useful in the diagnosis of diverticulosis, colorectal cancer, or inflammatory bowel disease. Delaying surgical exploration in order to pursue further imaging studies is not appropriate given the patient’s clinical presentation, which is suggestive of appendicitis with appendiceal rupture. Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy and observation (Choice C) are appropriate treatment options for uncomplicated appendicitis in select patients. This strategy is not appropriate in gravid patients and is associated with a lower success rate compared to surgical appendectomy, which remains the standard of care. Surgical exploration is mandatory once appendiceal perforation is suspected or has occurred.

questionStem: A previously healthy 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal cramps. Her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago. She is sexually active with one partner, and they use condoms for contraception consistently. She takes no medications. Her pulse is 90/min, and blood pressure is 100/65 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a soft abdomen and lower quadrant tenderness. Speculum examination shows moderate vaginal bleeding and a closed cervical os. A pregnancy test is positive. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows a fluid-filled endometrial cavity and no gestational sac. Her quantitative serum β-hCG concentration is 2500 mIU/mL. Forty-eight hours later, a second measurement of quantitative serum β-hCG concentration is 2800 mIU/mL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Pregnancy is suspected when there is a missed or delayed menstrual period, and ectopic pregnancy often presents with vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain. Serum β-hCG is produced by the placenta, is undetectable in nonpregnant patients, and doubles approximately every 48 hours during an early normal pregnancy. Ectopic pregnancy is an abnormal pregnancy in which the fertilized ovum implants in the fallopian tube (most common), on the ovary, within the peritoneal cavity, or in any non-endometrial location. β-hCG concentration does not increase as expected in ectopic pregnancy, often lagging the normal expected doubling. Ultrasonography can be used to assess for an intrauterine pregnancy and may show an ectopic pregnancy; in a normal pregnancy, an intrauterine gestational sac should be visible by 5 weeks' gestation. Additionally, transvaginal ultrasonography provides sufficient sensitivity to detect an intrauterine pregnancy once the β-hCG concentration exceeds 1000 to 2000 mIU/mL. An ectopic pregnancy is not viable. Treatment of an ectopic pregnancy can be medical with methotrexate for small, early pregnancies, but may require salpingectomy or evacuation with laparoscopy for larger pregnancies or in cases of medical treatment failure. Complications of ectopic pregnancy include rupture, bleeding, and hemoperitoneum.
incorrectExplanation: Blighted ovum (Choice A) is an anembryonic pregnancy in which a fertilized egg attaches to the uterine wall and a gestational sac without an embryo develops. It may present with vaginal bleeding or may be asymptomatic, and serum β-hCG concentration decreases with time. A complete spontaneous abortion (Choice B) would also present with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding with a delayed menstrual period. However, serum β-hCG concentration should decrease, not increase, with a spontaneous abortion. Hydatidiform mole (Choice D) is a form of gestational trophoblastic disease characterized by non-invasive diffuse swelling of chorionic villi and the absence of fetal parts in the case of a complete mole. Complete moles contain purely paternal DNA. On ultrasonography, there may be an enlarged uterus with cystic structures without any specific fetal structures. Hydatidiform moles produce β-hCG often in excess of proportion to gestational dates, which can be used as a biomarker. A normal intrauterine pregnancy (Choice E) may also present with abdominal pain and light vaginal bleeding or spotting in the first trimester due to implantation or threatened abortion. In a normal intrauterine pregnancy, serum β-hCG concentration should double in 48 hours.

questionStem: A 17-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because she has never had a menstrual period. She is otherwise healthy. Both of her older sisters had normal pubertal development. Examination shows absent breast development and scant pubic hair. Her serum follicle-stimulating hormone concentration is 105 mIU/mL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.D: Measurement of serum luteinizing hormone concentration
choices.E: Measurement of serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration

correctExplanation: Turner syndrome is a common cause of primary amenorrhea, which is caused by ovarian dysgenesis in a 45, XO genotype. Other signs of Turner syndrome include a short stature, cystic hygroma or webbed neck, swelling in the hands or feet, coarctation of the aorta, bicuspid aortic valve, horseshoe kidney, and infertility. Additionally, due to decreased estrogen concentration, patients fail to develop secondary sexual characteristics. Vital signs will be within normal limits, and diagnosis is made through a karyotype analysis. Increased concentrations of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) due to the lack of negative feedback from estrogen may also aid in diagnosis, but these findings are nonspecific.
incorrectExplanation: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) stimulation test (Choice A) can be used to diagnose central precocious puberty (< 8 years in girls and < 9 years in boys) or, occasionally, delayed puberty. After giving a GnRH analog to patients, LH and FSH concentrations are measured. Turner syndrome is a form of hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, and a GnRH-releasing stimulation test would not play a role in diagnosis. Measurement of serum electrolyte concentrations (Choice C) would not assist in the diagnosis of Turner syndrome as it is not characterized by serum electrolyte abnormalities. Measurement of serum luteinizing hormone concentration (Choice D) would be helpful in determining whether the patient's primary amenorrhea was hypergonadotropic or hypogonadotropic. However, it would not aid in the diagnosis of this patient, as the increased concentration of FSH already suggests hypergonadotropic hypogonadism. Measurement of serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration (Choice E) would aid in the diagnosis of thyroid disorders. While both hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism can present with irregular menses, they are uncommon causes of primary amenorrhea.

questionStem: A 26-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, comes for her first prenatal visit at 11 weeks' gestation. Her previous pregnancies and deliveries were uncomplicated. Her blood type is O, Rh-negative. She received Rh(D) immune globulin after her first delivery. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to evaluate her Rh status?
correctExplanation: The indirect antiglobulin (Coombs) test is conducted by combining red blood cells that contain the antigen of choice with the patient's serum. If the patient's serum contains antibodies against the antigen, in this case the blood antigen Rh, the antibodies will bind to the red blood cells. When Coombs reagent, or antiglobulin antibody, is added, the red blood cells will agglutinate. When an Rh-negative mother delivers a baby that is Rh-positive, it is possible that Rh antigens from the baby's blood can enter the maternal circulation and cause the mother's immune system to form antibodies against the Rh antigen. While this carries no significant complication with the initial exposure, a subsequent pregnancy with an Rh-positive fetus can result in severe hemolytic anemia of the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis) as the mother's antibodies can cross the placenta, causing hemolysis of the fetus's red blood cells. Rh(D) immune globulin (RhoGAM) acts by binding to Rh-positive cells that enter the maternal circulation, preventing the immune system from developing antibodies to the Rh antigen. Therefore, the best way to determine whether the mother has been exposed to Rh-positive blood and subsequently formed anti-Rh antibodies is the indirect antiglobulin (Coombs) test.
incorrectExplanation: Determination of the husband's Rh genotype (Choice A) would be useful in determining whether the patient was at risk for developing anti-Rh antibodies. If the father of her child was also Rh-negative, the child would subsequently be Rh-negative, and the mother would not be at risk of developing antibodies to Rh. However, as she has already had children, his genotype will not give information about her Rh antibody status. Measurement of fetal hemoglobin concentration (Choice B) is a useful measurement following birth when there is concern for hemolytic anemia of the newborn to determine the severity of hemolysis. However, measurement of the hemoglobin concentration of an 11-week-old fetus would not provide information on the mother's Rh antibody status given her previous pregnancies. Measurement of serum bilirubin concentration (Choice C) is also a useful marker of hemolysis. However, this mother is not at risk for hemolysis. Erythroblastosis fetalis causes hemolysis of the fetal blood; measurement of fetal serum bilirubin would be dangerous and risk fetal death at 11 weeks' gestation. Furthermore, it provides no information on the mother's Rh antibody status. Kleihauer-Betke acid elution test (Choice E) is used to quantify the amount of fetal blood to which the maternal circulation has been exposed in order to determine adequacy of Rh(D) immune globulin dosing. It is frequently used when an Rh-negative mother gives birth to an Rh-positive child. However, it would not give information on the patient's Rh antibody status.

questionStem: A 19-year-old primigravid woman comes to the emergency department because of a 1-week history of nausea and persistent vomiting. Her last menstrual period was 15 weeks ago, but she has had daily vaginal bleeding for the past month. She has not received prenatal care. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. Examination shows pedal edema. Pelvic examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 20-week gestation; there is no adnexal tenderness. A serum pregnancy test is positive. Urinalysis shows 1+ protein. Ultrasonography shows bilateral multilocular ovarian cysts and echogenic structures in the uterus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Hydatidiform moles are either caused by the fertilization of an empty egg by a single sperm followed by duplication of the paternal DNA resulting in 46 chromosomes (complete) or the dual fertilization of a normal ovum resulting in 69 chromosomes (incomplete). Maternal symptoms include hyperemesis gravidarum or persistent nausea and vomiting related to an abnormally increased β-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) concentration. They can also cause first trimester vaginal bleeding, early preeclampsia, and uterine size greater than expected for dates. Complete moles contain no fetal tissue, while incomplete contain some fetal tissue. However, neither are viable pregnancies and no fetal heartbeat will be found on Doppler ultrasonography. Pelvic examination may show cystic molar clusters in the vagina, and laboratory studies will show an abnormally increased β-hCG concentration. Ultrasonography of the pelvis will also show bilateral multilocular ovarian cysts (theca-lutein cysts) and echogenic structures in the uterus (hydatidiform molesy), as seen in this patient. Hydatidiform moles are treated with dilation and curettage, followed by appropriate contraception and sequential measurement of β-hCG to monitor for the development of malignant gestational trophoblastic diseases such as invasive moles or choriocarcinoma. These malignant diseases are treated with chemotherapy.
incorrectExplanation: Combined ectopic and intrauterine pregnancy (Choice A), also known as a heterotopic pregnancy, is extremely rare. It would likely present with abdominal pain and potential vaginal bleeding related to the ectopic extrauterine pregnancy. Ectopic pregnancies most commonly present early in pregnancy because of a restricted area for fetal development. An ultrasonography in this situation would show a viable intrauterine pregnancy in addition to an extrauterine ectopic pregnancy, most commonly in the fallopian tube. Multiple gestations (Choice C) can also present with hyperemesis gravidarum due to the increased maternal serum β-hCG concentration. However, ultrasonography would show more than one viable fetus in the uterus. Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (Choice D) is an exaggerated follicular response to injected gonadotropins commonly used in infertility treatment. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, and fluid retention, as well as shortness of breath and blood clots in severe cases. As this patient has not received injectable gonadotropins, this diagnosis is unlikely. Placenta accreta (Choice E) refers to the abnormal attachment of the placenta to the myometrium, rather than just the endometrium. Risk factors include prior cesarean delivery or uterine surgery, increased maternal age, and multiparity. Complications include postpartum hemorrhage due to the increased risk for retained products of conception. Polyhydramnios (Choice F) is an excessive amount of amniotic fluid. It is associated with maternal diabetes, multiple gestations, and fetal malformations such as esophageal or duodenal atresia and anencephaly. However, it is most commonly asymptomatic and would be associated with a viable uterine pregnancy, which is not seen in this patient.

questionStem: A previously healthy 42-year-old woman comes to the physician because of irregular menses during the past 7 months. She also has had intense mood changes and occasional hot flashes during this time. Her last menstrual period was 6 weeks ago. She is sexually active with one male partner, and they usually use barrier contraception. Examination, including pelvic examination, shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Pregnancy should be considered as a cause of irregular menses in all women of reproductive age, especially in patients with irregular use of contraceptives. Pregnancy may be accompanied by symptoms including mood changes and hot flashes. In women with advanced maternal age, pregnancy must be excluded as a potential cause by obtaining a pregnancy test before proceeding with further evaluation of other causes such as menopause.
incorrectExplanation: Measurement of serum estradiol (Choice A) and testosterone concentrations (Choice B) may detect hormonal changes associated with pregnancy or with disorders such as polycystic ovary syndrome, pituitary adenoma, or sex cord stromal tumors. A pregnancy test should be conducted before these conditions are considered. Transvaginal ultrasonography (Choice D) is useful for the evaluation of some causes of irregular menstruation, such as polycystic ovary syndrome or ovarian tumors. While transvaginal ultrasonography may identify an intrauterine pregnancy, a pregnancy test is a more sensitive initial test. Endometrial biopsy (Choice E) is useful for the evaluation of endometrial malignancy. In women of reproductive age, pregnancy must be excluded as a cause of irregular menstruation before considering more invasive diagnostic measures.

questionStem: A 24-year-old primigravid woman at 42 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital for labor induction. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated. She has no history of serious illness. On admission, her temperature is 36.9°C (98.5°F), pulse is 64/min, and blood pressure is 130/72 mm Hg. Fetal nonstress testing is reactive. Pelvic examination shows a closed, long, posterior cervix. The amniotic fluid index is 3.2 cm (N=9–31). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Discharge home and readmit in 1 week

correctExplanation: A pregnancy is considered postterm once a gestation extends to or beyond 42 weeks. Postterm pregnancy is associated with increased rates of maternal and neonatal complications, including meconium aspiration and fetal demise. While expectant management may be offered to select patients, the presence of an unfavorable cervix or oligohydramnios, as suggested by a low amniotic fluid index, are indications for induction of labor. Oligohydramnios may result from changes in maternal fetal circulation that occur because of the aging of the placenta. This is a known complication of postterm pregnancy and is associated with complications like umbilical cord compression. Induction of labor can be achieved by administering a prostaglandin analogue (eg. dinoprostone or misoprostol) or oxytocin. Nonpharmacologic methods of induction include stripping of the membranes and rupture of the amniotic sac.
incorrectExplanation: Discharging the patient home and readmitting in 1 week (Choice A) is inappropriate given the presence of oligohydramnios in a postterm pregnancy. While uncomplicated postterm pregnancies may be managed expectantly, the presence of complications such as oligohydramnios is an indication for the induction of labor to reduce the risk of maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality. Administration of betamethasone (Choice B), a corticosteroid that stimulates fetal lung maturation and promotes fetal lung production of surfactant, is appropriate in preterm pregnancies. It has no role in the management of complicated postterm pregnancy. Amnioinfusion (Choice D) is the process of instilling fluid into the amniotic cavity. Amnioinfusion may be useful for the management of oligohydramnios, especially when fetal heart rate monitoring reveals variable decelerations suggestive of umbilical cord compression. In this case, amnioinfusion does not address the underlying cause of oligohydramnios, which is postterm pregnancy and maternal fetal circulatory changes caused by aging of the placenta. Induction of labor is therefore a more appropriate next step in management. Immediate cesarean delivery (Choice E) exposes the mother and fetus to unnecessary risks associated with surgery. Induction of labor is a more appropriate initial step. Immediate cesarean delivery is indicated if the induction of labor leads to fetal distress. Educational Objective: Postterm pregnancy is defined as a gestation that persists to or beyond 42 weeks and is associated with maternal and fetal complications. The presence of an unfavorable cervix or of complications such as oligohydramnios are indications for the induction of labor, which is achieved with a prostaglandin analogue (eg, dinoprostone or misoprostol) or with oxytocin.

questionStem: A 23-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, at 26 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. She reports that her daughter had a flu-like illness 2 months ago that resolved without medical treatment. Her pregnancy has been otherwise uncomplicated, and results of prenatal laboratory studies have been within the reference ranges. Examination shows a fundal height of 34 cm. Ultrasonography shows polyhydramnios, fetal ascites, and skin thickening. Infection with which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
correctExplanation: Polyhydramnios, fetal ascites, and skin thickening caused by subcutaneous edema are characteristic of hydrops fetalis. Hydrops fetalis is diagnosed by the combination of fluid accumulation in at least two extravascular compartments (eg, pericardial effusion, pleural effusion, ascites, or subcutaneous edema). It is also associated with placentomegaly and polyhydramnios. There are various causes of hydrops fetalis, including iron deficiency anemia, twin-twin transfusion syndrome, maternal hyperthyroidism, erythroblastosis fetalis, hemolytic disease, and parvovirus B19. Parvovirus B19 infection in a gravid woman is associated with spontaneous abortion and fetal nonimmune hydrops fetalis. Symptoms of parvovirus B19 infection in children can include fever, upper respiratory tract symptoms, headache, and rash, which is usually self-limited. Adults may present with a viral prodrome and arthralgias.
incorrectExplanation: Adenovirus (Choice A) is a common virus that causes upper respiratory tract symptoms, fever, sore throat, and conjunctivitis. It does not have known deleterious fetal effects. Coxsackievirus A (Choice B) is an enterovirus that causes hand, foot, and mouth disease characterized by fever, painful blisters in the mouth and throat, and a macular rash especially on the hands and feet. Similar to adenovirus, it does not have known deleterious fetal effects. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) (Choice C) can often be asymptomatic or cause a short, febrile, flu-like illness. The risk for neonatal CMV infection is higher with a primary maternal infection than with recurrent infection. CMV is associated with intrauterine growth restriction, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, microcephaly, seizures, periventricular calcifications, and rash. Fetal hydrops is a potential complication of CMV infection, but parvovirus B19 infection is the more likely cause. Herpes simplex virus infection (Choice D) in an adult is characterized by tender vesicles with ulceration followed by crusting. It may pass to a newborn during delivery secondary to an ascending infection following spontaneous rupture of membranes or from passage through the infected lower genital tract. To prevent neonatal infection, acyclovir can be used to suppress outbreaks. A cesarean delivery is required if herpetic lesions or symptoms are present on the cervix, vagina, or vulva at the time of labor. Neonatal encephalitis is a severe complication.

questionStem: An 18-year-old woman comes to the physician because of irregular menses over the past 3 months; menses occur at 14- to 40-day intervals. Menstrual flow varies from spotting to heavy cramping and bleeding; the latter symptoms have caused her to miss school. Her last menstrual period was 3 weeks ago. Menarche was at the age of 12 years, and menses had occurred at regular 28-day intervals for 6 years. She has a sedentary lifestyle. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 63 kg (139 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m². Pelvic examination shows no abnormalities. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Cyclic progesterone therapy is a key treatment in the management of anovulation. Common causes of anovulation include pregnancy, polycystic ovary syndrome, abnormalities or immaturity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, menopause or premature ovarian failure, inadequate nutrition, chromosomal abnormalities, and thyroid disorders. Anovulation presents with irregular intervals of menstruation associated with heavy vaginal bleeding when menses occur because of continued endometrial development. Progesterone therapy acts to inhibit follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH), preventing ovulation. Progesterone therapy also maintains the endometrial lining and causes its transition to a secretory, rather than proliferative, endometrium. When progesterone is withdrawn, bleeding occurs if the anovulation is caused by an abnormality or irregularity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, as is often the case in young women. Bleeding will not occur if the anovulation is caused by a structural abnormality of the uterus or estrogen deficiency.
incorrectExplanation: Conjugated estrogen therapy (Choice A) is typically used to treat the vasomotor symptoms associated with menopause. Conjugated estrogen therapy is associated with an increased risk of breast cancer, hypercoagulability, and cardiovascular morbidity/mortality. It is also associated with endometrial cancer when used without progestins and would not be effective in treating this patient's anovulation. Hysteroscopy (Choice C) would be useful to evaluate the uterus for structural causes of irregular menses. However, this patient's symptoms are more consistent with anovulation than with polyps or fibroids, and hysteroscopy would not be the most useful next diagnostic step. Endometrial biopsy (Choice D) is recommended when a patient presents with postmenopausal bleeding with an increased thickness of the endometrium on ultrasonography, raising concern for endometrial hyperplasia and possible carcinoma. It does not play a role in a young patient with anovulatory bleeding. Dilation and curettage (Choice E) is useful in treating heavy or abnormal uterine bleeding that does not respond to less invasive interventions, as well as for removing fetal tissue or retained products of conception. It would not be the best next step, as there are less invasive initial options. Educational Objective: Cyclic progesterone therapy is frequently used to treat anovulatory irregular menses. It functions to transition the endometrium from the proliferative to secretory phase and inhibits FSH and LH secretion to prevent ovulation. When discontinued, bleeding will occur if the anovulation is related to irregular gonadotropin release, but it will not occur if there is a structural abnormality of the uterus or estrogen deficiency.

questionStem: A 37-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. Six weeks ago, a Pap smear showed low-grade intraepithelial lesions. She has had no symptoms and takes no medications. She is sexually active with one partner and uses a diaphragm for contraception. Examination shows a normal vagina, cervix, and uterus. Colposcopic examination shows an acetowhite area with punctation. The entire squamocolumnar junction cannot be visualized. A biopsy specimen of the cervix shows cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) 3. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Monthly Pap smears over the next 3 months

correctExplanation: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) 3 is a high-grade cervical lesion with an increased risk of progression to cervical cancer. Cervical carcinoma is classically associated with infection from human papillomavirus (HPV) high-risk strains 16, 18, 31, and 33. Risk factors include multiple sexual partners, smoking, and immunosuppression. Screening Pap smears are recommended every 3 years in women aged 21 to 29 years and every 5 years in conjunction with HPV co-testing (every three years if co-testing is not performed) in women aged 30 to 65 years. Abnormal Pap smear cytology results are most commonly evaluated by colposcopy, which allows for the visual assessment and biopsy of abnormal lesions. A colposcopy is deemed inadequate if the entirety of the squamocolumnar junction or transformation zone is not visible, as there is a possibility of undiagnosed carcinoma. In this case, the biopsy confirms CIN 3, which requires excision via a cone biopsy of the cervix (also known as cold knife conization). The cone biopsy serves to further evaluate a larger region of the cervix for cervical carcinoma and may be curative if a margin of normal cervical tissue is identified on histology. A loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) could alternatively be performed.
incorrectExplanation: Monthly Pap smears over the next 3 months (Choice A) and a second colposcopy in 3 months (Choice B) would delay definitive evaluation and treatment of this patient's CIN 3 without complete visualization of the entire transformation zone, which requires excision biopsy with either a cone biopsy or LEEP. Hysteroscopy (Choice C) would allow visualization of the uterine cavity and is useful in diagnosing endometrial polyps or performing endometrial biopsies. It does not typically play a role in the diagnosis or management of cervical carcinoma. Cryotherapy of the cervix (Choice E) would be appropriate therapy for CIN 2 or 3, or for persistent CIN 1. However, it is not an appropriate therapy for CIN 3 when the entire transformation zone was not visualized because the risk of unrecognized cervical carcinoma is high. Vaginal hysterectomy (Choice F) is a potential treatment option for recurrent CIN 2 or 3, as well as cervical carcinoma. However, it is important initially to fully evaluate the entirety of the cervical transformation zone via cone biopsy.

questionStem: A 12½-year-old girl is brought to the physician because she has not had a menstrual period for 5 months. Menarche was at the age of 11 years, and menses had occurred at irregular 30- to 90-day intervals and lasted 1 to 5 days. She plays softball in the spring and participates in physical education class at school two times weekly. She is not sexually active. She is at the 60th percentile for height and 40th percentile for weight. Examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Normal development of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis takes time. It is not uncommon for adolescent girls to have irregular periods for the first one to two years after beginning menstruation. This is due to immaturity of the HPO axis that results in irregular and noncyclic gonadotropin-releasing hormone release from the hypothalamus. This causes varying follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) concentrations, leading to anovulation and amenorrhea. This also affects the concentrations of estrogen and progesterone in the body, resulting in varying degrees of secondary sexual characteristic progression.
incorrectExplanation:
Anorexia nervosa (Choice A) can present with amenorrhea due to effects of malnutrition on cyclic gonadotropin release. However, it also presents with low body weight (BMI < 18.5 kg/m²), lanugo, and electrolyte imbalances, which are not seen in this patient.

Athletic amenorrhea (Choice B) is due to the suppression of the HPO axis with increased energy demands, leading to the decreased production of gonadotropin-releasing hormone. It occurs most commonly in thin females that are undergoing rigorous exercise or training regimens and would not be expected with this patient's average amount of exercise.

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) (Choice C) is a disorder of cortisol synthesis that has variable effects on mineralocorticoids and androgens. Symptoms include virilization, ambiguous genitalia, salt-wasting, hirsutism, precocious puberty, and abnormal uterine bleeding, depending on the subtype. It would be a less likely cause of oligomenorrhea in this young, otherwise healthy patient.

Hyperthyroidism (Choice D) presents with heat intolerance, palpitations, weight loss, diaphoresis, diarrhea, and amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea. This patient does not show any additional signs to suggest hyperthyroidism.

Hypothyroidism (Choice E) presents with weight gain, fatigue, constipation, cold intolerance, and occasionally with heavy or irregular periods. Physical examination typically discloses bradycardia, dry, edematous skin, and delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes. This patient does not show any additional signs to suggest hypothyroidism.

Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) (Choice F) most commonly presents with hirsutism, increased body weight, and irregular menses due to anovulation because of increased androgen concentration. Ultrasonography of the abdomen will show multiple intraparenchymal follicular cysts. This patient's presentation is more consistent with normal development.

A prolactin-secreting tumor (Choice G), most commonly in the pituitary gland, can secrete high enough concentrations of prolactin to inhibit gonadotropin-releasing hormone as well as FSH and LH. It can present with amenorrhea but is often associated with galactorrhea and would be less common cause of amenorrhea than normal development in this patient.

questionStem: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother due to concerns about irregular menses. The patient had her first menstrual period 6 months ago and has had 3 periods since then. She has no other medical problems and takes no medications. The patient is at the 50th percentile for height and weight. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

questionStem: A 27-year-old primigravid woman at 38 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital in labor. She had spontaneous rupture of membranes 2 days ago. On arrival, her temperature is 39.1°C (102.3°F). The cervix is 100% effaced and 4 cm dilated; the vertex is at +1 station. Abdominal examination shows exquisite tenderness of the uterine fundus. Pelvic examination shows mucopurulent cervical discharge. The fetal heart rate is 180/min with good variability. Treatment with intravenous ampicillin and gentamicin is begun. Two hours after admission, the cervix remains 4 cm dilated. She undergoes cesarean delivery for arrest of active phase and delivers a healthy newborn. Six hours after delivery, the patient's temperature is 38.9°C (102°F). Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's fever?
correctExplanation: Endomyometritis is an acute polymicrobial infection of the uterine endometrium and myometrium with normal vaginal flora. Patients typically present with fever and severe tenderness of the uterine fundus. Risk factors for the development of endomyometritis include premature and prolonged rupture of membranes (greater than 18 hours), spontaneous or elective abortion, cesarean delivery, and placement of an intrauterine device. Physical examination findings include uterine tenderness on bimanual examination and mucopurulent discharge, along with fetal tachycardia on tocometry, a stress response to the maternal infection, and fever. Broad-spectrum antibiotics such as ampicillin and gentamicin are typically used to allow for appropriate coverage of the polymicrobial infection, which typically involves an array of gram-negative and anaerobic bacteria.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Chlamydia trachomatis (Choice A) is a sexually transmitted bacterium that can cause cervicitis, urethritis, epididymitis, and pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). The clinical presentation of C. trachomatis associated PID can include fever, vaginal discharge, and pelvic organ tenderness. However, the cervical discharge in PID is typically watery, and C. trachomatis infections are not usually related to the post-partum state or prolonged rupture of membranes, which places this patient at greater risk for endomyometritis.

Escherichia coli (Choice B) is the bacterium most commonly responsible for urinary tract infections. Urinary tract infections present with dysuria, frequency, urinary urgency, suprapubic tenderness, and, if the infection has ascended to the kidneys, fever and costovertebral tenderness related to pyelonephritis. Patients with urinary tract infections do not present with cervical discharge or tenderness of the uterine fundus.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Choice C) is a sexually transmitted bacterium that can cause cervicitis, urethritis, septic arthritis, and PID. PID induced by N. gonorrhoeae can present with fever, mucopurulent cervical discharge, and pelvic organ tenderness; however, N. gonorrhoeae infections are not usually related to the post-partum state or prolonged rupture of membranes, which places this patient at greater risk for endomyometritis.

Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis (Choice E) is a rare sequela of endometritis that can lead to local invasion and infection of the pelvic vein walls, which causes intimal damage and thrombosis. This condition typically presents with pelvic pain and a fever that can be widely variable in range. Diagnosis typically occurs through blood cultures. If this patient were persistently febrile despite appropriate antibiotic treatment for endometritis, septic pelvic thrombophlebitis should be considered.

Educational Objective: Endomyometritis is typically a polymicrobial infection of the uterus from normal vaginal flora. In patients with postpartum fever, uterine tenderness, and pregnancy-related risk factors such as prolonged rupture of the membranes, endomyometritis should be suspected.

questionStem: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of painful vulvar swelling for 2 days. She has had three episodes of Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection treated successfully with oral antibiotics over the past 5 years. Examination shows a 4-cm, tender, fluctuant mass of the labium majus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: A Bartholin duct abscess can occur when a Bartholin gland becomes obstructed and infected. A Bartholin gland is located on each side of the introitus and provides secretions that lubricate the vagina. Occasionally, the ducts of these glands become obstructed, leading to a Bartholin cyst. This presents as a small area of painful, fluctuant swelling over the posterior aspect of the labium majus. With ongoing obstruction and inflammation, infection can develop, leading to a Bartholin gland abscess, marked by erythema and tenderness to palpation of the cyst. Abscesses are commonly polymicrobial, but Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a frequently isolated aerobe. They are treated with incision and drainage, often with placement of a catheter to promote complete evacuation.
incorrectExplanation: Bacterial vaginosis (Choice A) is an infection caused by Gardnerella vaginalis or overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria in the vagina, usually in women with frequent sexual activity or antibiotic use, although it is not sexually transmitted. Symptoms include thin, malodorous, gray-white discharge. It does not cause vulvar abscesses. Human papillomavirus (Choice C) is a sexually transmitted viral infection that can cause cervical, vulvar, penile, or anal carcinoma, as well as condylomata acuminata. It would not be expected to cause a vulvar abscess or labial swelling. Lichen sclerosus (Choice D) occurs in postmenopausal women with thinning and fibrosis of the skin of the genital and perianal areas. It presents with pruritic white plaques, occasionally with ulcerations, and carries an increased risk for squamous cell carcinoma of the vulva. It does not present with abscess formation. Urethral diverticulum (Choice E) is an outpouching of the urethra that presents with recurrent urinary tract infections, urethritis, urinary incontinence, and incomplete bladder emptying. It does not cause vulvar abscesses. It would not be expected to cause a vulvar abscess.

questionStem: A 47-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 4-day history of increasing pain with urination. Five days ago, she began treatment with a sulfonamide antibiotic by her primary physician after a phone consultation; she has not had relief of her symptoms. She has no history of serious illness, abnormal Pap smears, or sexually transmitted diseases. She currently takes no medications. She states that she has had increasing stress during the past month. Pelvic examination shows an exquisitely tender ulcer on the lower labium minus. A photograph of the lower labia is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1) genital infection is characterized by painful vesicles in the genital area (eg, vulva, vagina, cervix, perineum) and may be associated with pain during urination. Most cases of genital herpes are caused by HSV-2, however HSV-1 has also been associated with genital herpes infection. It typically begins with the formation of vesicles, which lyse and progress to shallow, painful ulcers with an erythematous border. This painful rash can be exacerbated during urination, in which acidic urine passes over open vesicles or ulcers. This dysuria may be misinterpreted for an underlying urinary tract infection, which may be treated with sulfonamide antibiotics, however, this would not be effective in treating HSV. HSV is treated with acyclovir or valacyclovir, which are guanosine analogs that inhibit viral DNA polymerase. This reduces the duration of viral shedding and symptoms.
incorrectExplanation: Vulvovaginal candidiasis (Choice A) presents with erythema, itching, burning, and excoriation in the vulval and vaginal tissues. Examination is characterized by thick, white, coarse discharge, and diagnosis is via pseudohyphae on microscopy. Risk factors include diabetes mellitus and recent antibiotic or corticosteroid use. It does not cause ulcerations or vesicles. Condyloma acuminatum (Choice B) are genital warts associated with human papillomavirus and can appear on the penis, vagina, vulva, and/or anal canal. Patients with HIV are prone to severe condyloma lesions in these regions. Condyloma acuminatum presents with soft, fleshy growths, and diagnosis is made with examination and/or biopsy. Molluscum contagiosum (Choice D), caused by poxvirus, is characterized by small painless papules with a central umbilication and may appear anywhere on the body. It is treated with cryotherapy or topical trichloroacetic acid and benzoyl peroxide. Paget disease (Choice E) of the vulva is a type of skin cancer that arises from glandular cells. It appears as a pink or red well-demarcated raised skin lesion that can be located on the vulva, perineum, or inner thigh. It can be pruritic; diagnosis is made with biopsy. Educational Objective: HSV-1 and HSV-2 can both cause genital herpes, characterized by painful vesicles and ulcers on an erythematous base. Symptoms typically include local pain and itching, dysuria, and tender lymphadenopathy.

questionStem: A 37-year-old woman, gravida 7, para 4, aborta 2, at 40 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital in labor. Spontaneous rupture of membranes along with severe abdominal pain occurred 4 hours ago. The pain is constant and sharp, unlike the labor pains of her previous pregnancies. Her pregnancy had been uncomplicated. Her last pregnancy ended in cesarean delivery at term for breech presentation. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 17/min, and blood pressure is 122/68 mm Hg. The fundal height is 28 cm. Leopold maneuvers show fetal small parts above the fundus. correctExplanation: Uterine rupture is a dangerous complication of pregnancy wherein the muscular wall of the uterus tears. Severe pain is a common initial finding. Hemodynamic instability can manifest in the mother with tachycardia and hypotension, and in the fetus with late decelerations, tachycardia, bradycardia, or loss of beat-to-beat variability. If uterine rupture occurs during labor, sudden loss of fetal station is a highly suggestive finding. Fetal parts may be palpable above the fundus with Leopold maneuvers. Risk factors for uterine rupture include vaginal birth after caesarean delivery, multiparity, and induction of labor with prostaglandin analogues or oxytocin. Uterine rupture is treated with emergency laparotomy.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Presenting findings include abdominal or pelvic pain, abnormal vaginal bleeding, and tetanic contractions. An abnormal fetal heart rate may be detected, and fetal demise may occur if the abruption is large. The uterine wall remains intact during placental abruption, and fetal parts will not be palpable above the fundus.

Chorioamnionitis (Choice B) is a bacterial infection of the fetal membranes that commonly occurs with premature or prolonged rupture of the membranes. Maternal fever and leukocytosis are characteristic, and the uterus may be tender to palpation.

Placenta previa (Choice C) is an abnormal positioning of placental tissue such that the placenta partially or entirely overlies the internal cervical os. Placenta previa is usually detected on routine prenatal ultrasonography. Its most common presenting symptom is third trimester painless vaginal bleeding.

Umbilical cord prolapse (Choice D) is an intrapartum complication wherein the fetal umbilical cord precedes the fetus into the cervical canal. The resulting compression of the umbilical vasculature can impair fetal oxygenation and may be immediately life threatening. Fetal bradycardia is a common presenting finding.

questionStem: A 22-year-old primigravid woman at 24 weeks' gestation has had fullness in the lower pelvic area for 12 hours. She has no contractions. Fundal height is 20 cm. Fetal heart tones are good. Examination shows the fetus in a breech presentation in the vagina. No cervix is palpated. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: The American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology defines cervical incompetence, or cervical insufficiency, as the inability of the cervix to contain the pregnancy (the fetus, placenta, and amniotic sac) without the presence of contractions, labor, or both, typically during the second or early third trimester. The condition is associated with spontaneous abortion, preterm or premature rupture of the membranes, and preterm birth. Classically, when symptomatic, it presents with feelings of fullness in the lower pelvis in the absence of contractions or labor. Speculum examination may show a dilated or effaced cervix, or protrusion of the pregnancy through the cervical os into the vagina, as in this example. Mild cases without dilation of the external os may go undetected. Cervical length measurements may reveal a shortened cervix, with a cervical length less than 15-25 mm. Treatment is indicated if the degree of cervical insufficiency is significant enough to threaten the pregnancy. This is accomplished through cervical cerclage, which is the placement of a suture into the cervical os to narrow the canal and maintain a closed cervix. The suture is then removed at the time of labor, or around 36 to 38 weeks' gestation.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, E, F, G, H, and I.

Cervical carcinoma (Choice B) is classically associated with infection from human papillomavirus high-risk strains 16, 18, 31, and 33. It presents indolently until advanced, locally invasive, or metastatic; vaginal bleeding or postcoital spotting may be the presenting symptom. Smoking, immunosuppression, and multiple sexual partners are risk factors.

Unless the placenta migrates away from the os, a cesarean delivery is generally required to prevent significant bleeding, as well as fetal or maternal death during childbirth.

Premature labor (Choice E) is defined as labor (regular contractions plus cervical change) occurring after 20 and prior to 37 weeks' gestation. The risk to fetal survival is greater the earlier preterm labor occurs.

Premature rupture of the membranes (Choice F) is the rupture of the amniotic sac before the onset of labor (regular contractions plus cervical change). Patients typically report a gush of fluid or steady leakage of fluid from the vagina. Complications include chorioamnionitis, preterm birth, cord compression, and postpartum endometritis.

Prolapsed cord (Choice G) is a complication of pregnancy in which the umbilical cord traverses the cervical os into the vagina ahead of the fetus, creating the risk of cord compression and fetal hypoxia. It is an obstetric emergency and is managed by positioning the mother to relieve cord compression, elevating any compressing fetal part, and emergency cesarean delivery.

Vaginal varicose veins (Choice H) are dilated, engorged, tortuous veins occurring because of increased venous hydrostatic pressure and decreased pelvic venous return as pregnancy progresses. Unless bleeding or thrombosis occurs, they have no significant pathologic consequence and resolve following delivery.

questionStem: A 37-year-old woman, gravida 5, para 3, aborta 1, at 40 weeks' gestation is admitted in labor. Contractions began 2 hours ago. She has not had vaginal bleeding or loss of fluid. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated. Her last child was delivered vaginally at term and weighed 4300 g (9 lb 8 oz). At her last prenatal visit 1 week ago, the cervix was 50% effaced and 1 cm dilated, and the vertex was at -2 station. Examination now shows contractions that occur every 5 minutes. The cervix is 50% effaced and 6 cm dilated; no presenting part can be felt. A fetal heart tracing shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Arterial blood gas analysis of the umbilical artery

correctExplanation: Ultrasonography of the pelvis would allow the clinician to determine the fetus's positioning when no presenting fetal part can be felt at the cervical opening. Fetal malpresentation occurs when any portion of the fetus besides the occiput presents at the cervical os. This malpresentation prevents the head from properly engaging in the pelvis for descent. In some cases, excess amniotic fluid (eg, polyhydramnios) can prevent any fetal part from presenting at the cervical os until the rupture of membranes occurs. A serious complication that can occur in fetal malpresentation is umbilical cord prolapse. Because of the lack of occiput engagement at the cervical os, the cord can protrude through the cervix following the rupture of membranes before the fetus descends into the pelvis. Further contractions can cause cord compression, and the cord can be impinged by the fetus, resulting in fetal hypoxia. Given the high risk associated with vaginal deliveries in cases of fetal malpresentation, cesarean delivery may be necessary. Cord prolapse, however, is an obstetric emergency, requiring immediate cesarean delivery.
incorrectExplanation: Arterial blood gas analysis of the umbilical artery (Choice A) is used to determine the oxygen levels and pH of the fetal circulation at the time of delivery. Hypoxia and acidosis can signify potentially severe hypoxic-ischemic injury to the fetus. However, this fetus is not in distress with a normal fetal heart tracing, making an arterial blood gas analysis of the umbilical artery unnecessary. Fetal scalp stimulation (Choice B) is useful in detecting metabolic abnormalities of the fetus, including acidemia, when there are signs of fetal distress. Forceps are used to stimulate the scalp, and an elevation in the heart rate of 15/min above baseline for 15 seconds is associated with normal fetal outcome. Amniotomy (Choice D) is manual rupture of the amniotic membrane. It is frequently used to induce labor. However, it would be dangerous to perform in this patient due to the risk of cord prolapse associated with fetal malpresentation. Cesarean delivery (Choice E) is generally indicated in fetal malpresentation. However, the best next step in management is to determine the fetal position with ultrasonography, rather than move directly to cesarean delivery prior to confirmation of the fetal lie, as vaginal delivery may still be an option. Educational Objective: Rupture of membranes when there is no palpable presenting fetal body part carries a high risk of cord prolapse, which can lead to cord compression and fetal hypoxia. Ultrasonography of the pelvis allows the clinician to assess the fetal position to determine appropriate management.

questionStem: A 27-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician because she has been unable to conceive for 3 years. Menses occur at irregular 35- to 42-day intervals and last 8 days. Laparoscopy 8 weeks ago showed spill from both fallopian tubes after methylene blue dye was instilled into the cervix; there was no evidence of endometriosis. Her husband has two children from a previous marriage. Pelvic examination shows a normal-sized uterus and no palpable masses. Postcoital test shows many motile sperm. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Clomiphene stimulates ovulation by acting as an estrogen receptor antagonist to block the negative feedback on gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) in the hypothalamus. Clomiphene thereby increases the downstream effects of GnRH. It is commonly used in women struggling with infertility due to anovulatory cycles. Anovulation presents with irregular intervals of menstruation, associated with heavy vaginal bleeding when menses occur due to continued endometrial development. Anovulation is caused by pregnancy, polycystic ovary syndrome, abnormalities or immaturity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, menopause or premature ovarian failure, inadequate nutrition, chromosomal abnormalities, and thyroid disorders. Other causes of infertility in women include fallopian tube blockage, structural abnormalities of the uterus, and thyroid disorders.
incorrectExplanation: Danazol (Choice B) acts as a synthetic androgen and partial androgen receptor agonist to prevent the ovary from secreting estradiol. It is used in endometriosis but has no role in infertility management. Leuprolide (Choice C) is structurally similar to GnRH. When used in a pulsatile manner, it stimulates the downstream effects of GnRH, leading to ovulation. However, when used continuously, it acts as a GnRH antagonist to downregulate follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) release. Unlike clomiphene, which is oral, leuprolide is an injectable medication, making it less ideal for initial pharmacotherapy. Levothyroxine (Choice D) is used to treat hypothyroidism, which can present with anovulation and oligomenorrhea. However, symptoms also include bradycardia, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, and depressed mood, none of which affect this patient. Menotropins (Choice E) are also used in infertility treatment, although to a lesser degree with the advent of newer medications. They are mixtures of gonadotropins (FSH and LH) obtained from the urine of postmenopausal women, in whom such hormones are present in higher concentration. They stimulate the production and differentiation of ovarian follicles, but are also administered by injection, making them less useful for initial pharmacotherapy. Progesterone (Choice F) therapy in anovulation is commonly used to control irregular bleeding. However, it would prevent fertility in this patient through negative feedback on the pituitary gland.

questionStem: A 21-year-old primigravid woman at 10 weeks' gestation has had severe nausea and has been unable to keep anything in her stomach for 48 hours. She has had mild nausea and vomiting for 6 weeks. Examination shows normal findings. Ultrasonography shows a normal 10-week gestation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Severe nausea with inability to maintain adequate oral intake is a common presenting symptom of hyperemesis gravidarum (HG) and can lead to clinically significant dehydration and starvation ketosis, which can be assessed through the measurement of urinary ketones. HG is usually associated with weight loss in early pregnancy and extends past the first trimester, when typical morning sickness resolves. Tachycardia, mild hypotension, and signs of dehydration (eg, dry mucous membranes) would be expected on vital signs and physical examination. Results of laboratory studies show ketones in the blood and urine, and depending on the degree of severity, electrolyte, volume, and acid/base abnormalities (eg, hyposmolar hyponatremia, hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis, metabolic acidosis) caused by vomiting, dehydration, ketogenesis, and severe volume contraction. As HG is commonly associated with molar pregnancy, it is also important to check a β-human chorionic gonadotropin concentration and obtain a pelvic ultrasonography. Treatment of HG includes vitamin B6 supplementation, intravenous fluids, antiemetics, and in severe cases, total parenteral nutrition.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Complete blood count (Choice A) would not necessarily be affected by hyperemesis gravidarum or prolonged nausea and vomiting. While leukocytosis could be associated with an infectious cause of gastrointestinal distress, infection is less likely in this patient than HG given the prolonged nature of her symptoms and association with pregnancy. Volume contraction may be reflected by increased hematocrit.

Measurement of serum bilirubin concentration (Choice B) would be appropriate in suspected cases of hemolysis, liver disease (eg, hepatitis), or preeclampsia, any of which could cause nausea and vomiting. For example, acute hepatitis classically presents with nausea, vomiting, jaundice, increased transaminases, and right upper quadrant pain. This patient has no reported risk factors for exposure to hepatitis, and HG is more likely.

Measurement of serum glucose concentration (Choice C) may provide additional information on the adequacy of oral intake, nutritional reserves, and the possibility of gestational diabetes. However, changes in serum glucose would be nonspecific and would not establish the diagnosis.

Measurement of urinary protein (Choice E) would be indicated for the evaluation of nephrotic syndrome, nephritic syndrome, and preeclampsia. Urinary ketones are more specific in HG, and urine protein is not necessarily increased.

Educational Objective: Hyperemesis gravidarum presents with severe, often intractable nausea and vomiting, preventing adequate oral intake in a pregnant patient with subsequent dehydration and starvation. Associated findings include ketonuria and ketonemia, electrolyte abnormalities, acid/base disturbances, and volume contraction. Treatment consists of vitamin B6 supplementation, intravenous fluids, antiemetics, and possible total parenteral nutrition.

questionStem: An otherwise healthy 27-year-old woman comes to the physician 2 weeks after noticing a tender mass in her left breast during breast self-examination. She has a history of similar smaller masses that resolved spontaneously within a few weeks. She feels well and takes no medications. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals. Her last menstrual period was 3½ weeks ago. Vital signs are within normal limits. There is no lymphadenopathy. The breasts are symmetric, and there are no skin changes. Examination of the left breast shows several 1-cm, smooth, soft, mobile masses and a 3-cm, mobile, soft, tender mass in the upper outer quadrant. Examination of the right breast shows tenderness to deep palpation and small masses similar to the left breast. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Fibrocystic changes of the breast occur most commonly in premenopausal women over the age of 35 but can also occur in younger patients of reproductive age, such as in in this case. Patients may present with various sites of breast pain and lumps unilaterally or bilaterally. The condition is characterized by the presence of cysts, stromal fibrosis, and apocrine metaplasia on histology, and it is believed to occur in response to hormonal fluctuations during the menstrual cycle. On examination, the cysts may appear blue. Fibrocystic change is a benign disease and does not generally convey an increased risk of cancer (with the exception of certain subtypes). However, it can result in recurrent mastalgia. If there is associated discomfort, aspiration can be performed, which may relieve symptoms. Cyst aspiration can yield fluid that is clear, milky, yellow, green, or brown, which are all likely benign. Supportive care, using nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications and a well-fitting brassiere is also appropriate. Oral contraceptive therapy has not generally been shown to relieve symptoms of fibrocystic breast disease or cyclic breast pain.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, E, F, G, H, and I.

Abscess (Choice A) is often a complication of mastitis. Breast abscesses commonly occur in breastfeeding women, and present with a localized region of indurated, fluctuant, erythematous, and tender tissue.

Fat necrosis (Choice B) is often detected in the breast as a palpable nodularity in an area of previous trauma. On imaging, peripheral calcifications are often seen.

Fibroadenoma (Choice C) presents as a unilateral, nontender, mobile, rubbery mass in the breast, often in a younger woman. It is typically benign.

Galactocele (Choice E) is a retained collection of breast milk that presents as a painless breast lump, typically following the cessation of lactation. Galactoceles generally self-resolve.

Intraductal papillomas (Choice F) are the most common cause of unilateral bloody nipple discharge. They are benign tumors originating from the walls of lactiferous ducts and can be solitary or multiple.

Lipoma (Choice G) describes benign neoplasia of adipocytes, and generally presents as a solitary, painless, soft, mobile, subcutaneous mass, often on the torso.

Mammary ductal ectasia (Choice H) often occurs in perimenopausal women and refers to a widening of the lactiferous ducts, often near the nipple. Ectatic ducts are often asymptomatic until they become blocked, at which time they may become nodular or painful.

Mastitis (Choice I) presents with erythema and induration of the breast in an area of tender, warm skin. It classically occurs in breast-feeding mothers as a result of nipple trauma leading to inoculation from cutaneous or oral flora.
