questionStem: A 37-year-old primigravid woman at 31 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. She reports a 4-day history of mild difficulty breathing, especially when in the reclining position. She has no history of serious illness; her only medication is a prenatal vitamin. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. The fundal height is 37 cm. Pelvic examination shows no cervical dilation or effacement. Ultrasonography shows a normal-appearing fetus. The amniotic fluid index is 35 cm (N=10–20). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Recommendation to limit dietary sodium intake
choices.E: Weekly amniocentesis for removal of fluid

correctExplanation: Polyhydramnios refers to excessive levels of amniotic fluid volume, increased uterine size relative to gestational age, and is associated with an increased risk of fetal anomalies, placental abruption, preterm labor, and postpartum uterine atony. It should be suspected when the uterine size and fundal height is larger than expected for gestational age. Polyhydramnios can be diagnosed on ultrasonography examination by measuring the amniotic fluid index (AFI). An AFI greater than 20 cm indicates an excessive amount of amniotic fluid. Polyhydramnios can be idiopathic or associated with a variety of disorders, including maternal diabetes mellitus, fetal infection with parvovirus B19, twin-twin transfusion syndrome, and fetal chromosomal or structural abnormalities (eg, esophageal or duodenal atresia, anencephaly). Fetal anomalies are the most common cause of polyhydramnios. Antenatal testing such as fetal ultrasonography with biophysical profile should be performed to evaluate for underlying fetal anomalies along with an amniocentesis to evaluate for chromosomal or genetic abnormalities if ultrasonography is nondiagnostic.
incorrectExplanation: Complete bed rest (Choice A) is not recommended for patients with polyhydramnios, as this would not improve the patient's pregnancy prognosis. Further testing should be performed to evaluate the fetus for structural or chromosomal abnormalities. The recommendation to limit dietary sodium intake (Choice B) and diuretic therapy (Choice D) have no role in the treatment of polyhydramnios. Maternal sodium intake or use of diuretic therapy would have minimal to no effect on the amount of amniotic fluid, as polyhydramnios is most commonly related to underlying fetal structural or chromosomal abnormalities. Weekly amniocentesis for removal of fluid (Choice E) is performed for patients with severe polyhydramnios causing severe shortness of breath or abdominal discomfort. Weekly amniocentesis would not be appropriate in this patient with mild difficulty breathing.

questionStem: A 77-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of intermittent episodes of vaginal bleeding. Each episode lasts 3 to 4 days and is not associated with trauma or sexual intercourse. Menopause occurred 26 years ago, and she has never received hormone therapy. Her last gynecologic examination was 38 years ago following the birth of her youngest child. She takes no medications. She has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 50 years. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Pelvic examination shows a 2-cm, exophytic lesion on the cervix. There is no enlargement of the uterus or evidence of blood in the vagina. Results of a biopsy specimen of the lesion are most likely to show which of the following?
correctExplanation: An exophytic lesion on the cervix is concerning for cervical cancer, which in about 70% of cases is squamous cell carcinoma derived from the epithelial lining of the ectocervix. Cervical squamous cell carcinoma begins from the transformation zone, or squamocolumnar junction, which demarcates the ectocervix and its squamous epithelium from the endocervix and its columnar epithelium. This region is the most likely initial site of cervical cancer development and is the target region of a Pap smear, a screening test for cervical neoplasia. Risk factors for cervical cancer include infection with human papillomavirus (HPV) high risk strains 16, 18, 31, or 33; early age at onset of sexual activity; tobacco use; oral contraceptive use; immunosuppression; and infection with HIV or other sexually transmitted infections. Cervical cancer classically presents with vaginal bleeding occurring with or without intercourse. It may locally invade into the bladder or rectum if advanced and can result in hydronephrosis by obstructing the distal ureteral insertion to the bladder. If distant spread occurs, the lung is a common site of metastatic disease.
incorrectExplanation: Adenocarcinoma (Choice A) is a less common type of cervical cancer. Compared to squamous cell carcinoma, it makes up approximately 25% of invasive cervical cancers. In most cases, cervical adenocarcinoma and cervical squamous cell carcinoma have the same treatment. Clear cell changes may also be seen in renal and endometrial cancers. Papillary serous carcinoma (Choice D) is a rare uterine malignancy. Compared to endometrial carcinoma, it has a higher propensity for lymphatic spread.

questionStem: A 27-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 30 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of chronic fatigue for 2 months; she has had a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss during this period. She has had no prenatal care. She has a history of alcoholism and drug abuse. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 59 kg (130 lb); BMI is 21 kg/m². She appears chronically ill. Examination shows pallor. The uterine fundal height is 28 cm. The fetal heart rate is 140/min. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 6.0 g/dL, Mean corpuscular hemoglobin 30 pg/cell, Mean corpuscular volume 101 µm³, Leukocyte count 4300/mm³, Reticulocyte count 0.1%, Platelet count 130,000/mm³, Prothrombin time 13 sec, Serum Bilirubin (total) 1.0 mg/dL, ALT 16 U/L. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's anemia?
correctExplanation: Folic acid deficiency is a common cause of megaloblastic anemia in pregnancy because of increased folic acid requirements, especially when accompanied by malnutrition due to alcohol use disorder. Other causes of megaloblastic anemia in pregnancy include malabsorption and certain medications. In this case, the anemia is caused by impaired DNA synthesis in the red blood cell progenitor cells due to the absence of required cofactors. Symptoms include fatigue, pallor, lightheadedness, and shortness of breath. Laboratory studies will show a decreased hemoglobin concentration, increased mean corpuscular volume, decreased reticulocyte count, increased homocysteine concentration, and normal methylmalonic acid concentration. Leukocyte and platelet counts are generally normal. Peripheral blood smear will show hypersegmented neutrophils. Treatment requires folic acid supplementation and red blood cell transfusion if severe.
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, E, and F. Bone marrow hypoplasia (Choice A) is a dysfunction of the bone marrow, leading to anemia, thrombocytopenia, and leukopenia, and is typically caused by radiation or chemotherapy, toxic chemicals (eg, heavy metals), medications, autoimmune disorders, or infections. This patient's leukocyte and platelet counts are normal, making bone marrow hypoplasia unlikely. Cirrhosis (Choice B) of the liver is associated with anemia, commonly caused by chronic blood loss into the gastrointestinal tract and subsequent iron deficiency or red blood cell sequestration resulting from splenomegaly in portal hypertension. If cirrhosis is caused by alcohol use disorder, folic acid deficiency may also result. However, cirrhosis also presents with ascites, jaundice, signs of portal hypertension, and increased prothrombin time and bilirubin, none of which are noted in this case. Hepatitis (Choice D) can be caused by viral infections, autoimmune diseases, medications, and alcohol use. However, hepatitis would generally cause increased transaminases, which are not seen in this case. Iron deficiency (Choice E) is a common cause of anemia. In gravid patients, this is typically due to increased metabolic demand for iron. It can also be caused by occult gastrointestinal bleeding, malabsorption, and malnutrition. However, it is a microcytic anemia and would present with decreased mean corpuscular volume.
